chapter: With Benny Goodman and Louis Armstrong
title: Oneida storm, Meadowbrook and Goodman's whistle
summary: Playing in storm conditions and at Frank Dailey's, Goodman whistled at Simmons to play softer.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: So they had a Blue Law there, you know. Couldn't work on Sundays. So, like, we worked Saturday nights, and we took a bus, chartered a bus, to Oneida, New York, a resort, upstate New York, and had an electrical storm. Oh, it rained. But this played havoc on my bass strings and Sid's drum heads. You know,

they drop and get out of tune very easily, you know, when it rains. And there was no air conditioning. They had one of these large restaurant fans, you know, one of those tall ones, in front of the bandstand. Beautiful shell, good acoustics, but it was burning up in there.

Mel Powell is on one end, and Lou McGarity is on the other end. And Mel Powell says, "Caw caw," signifying. And Lou McGarity would give it right back to him: "Caw caw." I'm picking a note, tuning, taking a tune. Benny says, "Come on." And I screamed back at him, "K M A," you know? So when we got off, he says, "What's wrong with your boy?" Sid says, "Phonograph" got to play the part of Clark Terry.

So we get back to Toronto, play that night, and we played without any words. And when we left there, we went to Frank Daly's, Meadowbrook. And the way the brass section that he had -- something like five trumpets, after you added Cootie with the band. Cootie didn't have a book. He'd just have to get up and play a solo, cold. You know. But he had Billy Butterfield, Jimmy Maxwell, couple of other trumpet players, I don't remember their names. And he had Lou McGarity and Cutty Cutshall playing trombones.

Now, the brass section, instead of patting their feet, they tromped, alternating from foot to foot, you know. Blump, blump, blump, blump, like they was marching. And Big Sid was pounding the cymbal to sound over them, and this is

making me give up all the strength that I've got, as small as I was, to be heard. I heard this whistling in the distance, like someone was hailing a cab. And looked up, and he's pointing at me to tell me to be quiet. WILLARD: Benny? Yeah, to play softer.
Now, you know my feathers dropped. I didn't feel like playing the rest of the night.
